transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Lara Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Gupta (Redwood Infra), Alice Romero (Zetta Eng Lead), Daniel Park (Zetta CTO), Priya Shah (Zetta SRE)
Links shared: prefix-cache-design-v1.pdf (Redwood drive), pilot-benchmarks-20250218.xlsx (sheet), security-snapshot.pdf

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategy. Goals: reduce token cost and tail latency for Zetta's multi-tenant chat API while ensuring tenant isolation and auditability in VPC/private deploys. Discussed cache key design, hit-rate targets, safety for multi-tenant workloads, eviction, metrics, and how caching interacts with batching/kv cache/quantization. Agreed next steps to share artifacts and run a 2-week pilot on Redwood Private pre-prod.

Topics: prefix caching hit rates, cache key schema, tenant isolation/namespace, TTL and eviction policies, measuring effective hit rate vs served tokens, interplay with KV cache and per-request batching, quantized model behavior when serving cached prefixes, VPC/on-prem constraints for network and KMS, instrumentation for monitoring cache correctness and staleness.

00:00 Lara: Alright, hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll kick off, I'm Lara from Redwood, AE on the account, quick intros please.
00:12 Alice: Hi Alice Romero, engineering lead on Zetta's conversation infra, we own the chat api.
00:17 Daniel: Daniel Park, CTO, I'll mostly observe but want to make sure we keep security in the loop.
00:24 Marcus: Marcus Patel, Redwood SE, I'll be the deep dive owner today.
00:29 Priya: Priya Shah, SRE, I'll be asking ops questions.
00:33 Samir: Samir Gupta, infra, responsible for VPN/VPC peering and networking.
00:40 Lara: Great. Marcus, take it away.
00:44 Marcus: Cool thanks. So quick framing: Zetta serves multi-tenant chat with long-lived conversations. You told us earlier that about 60% of requests have common system prompts and reused prefix fragments — that's low hanging fruit for prefix caching. Today we'll go through key design choices: what to include in the cache key, acceptable TTLs, multi-tenant isolation, and how we measure true hit rate. Also we'll cover how this interacts with our runtime's KV cache and batching.
01:12 Alice: Quick note — we do a lot of dynamic system prompts per customer, plus per-session personalization that gets appended.
01:21 Marcus: Right, so one main question: do you want tenant-shared cache entries for common system prompts or strict per-tenant namespaces?
01:28 Daniel: For compliance some customers require strict isolation. We can't accidentally serve another customer's prefix.
01:35 Priya: Also we want to be able to trace which tenant produced a cached output, for audit logs.
01:42 Marcus: Understood. Our recommended default: namespace cache by customer_id and optionally by route_id. Then provide an opt-in shared pool for public common prompts (e.g., open system instructions) with explicit consent. That way you get high hit rate for public prompts without violating tenant isolation.
01:59 Alice: How does that affect hit rate though, if we namespace everything? Our hit rate could drop a lot.
02:06 Marcus: Good point. In our early internal benchmarks we saw namespace-by-tenant reduces cross-tenant hits but you can still get high within-tenant reuse if customers have repetitive prompts. The tradeoff: per-tenant namespace means lower global hit rate but stronger safety. Shared pool improves global hit rate but requires policy and content classification.
02:27 Priya: Can we hash system prompt plus model+temp and still be safe?
02:33 Marcus: Yes, hashed keys are fine. Cache key suggestion we propose: sha256(prefix_payload) + model_id + model_config_signature (quantization tag, e.g., int8/fp16) + generation_params_hash (temperature/stop sequence) + tenant_namespace. So the full key is a concatenation of those components then hashed.
02:55 Alice: Wait, model_config_signature? If we quantize we might change tokenization or sampling.
03:02 Marcus: Exactly — quantization can change logits slightly and results could diverge. Keying by quantization profile avoids serving cached outputs produced by a different numeric precision. We also recommend including kernel/runtime-version so if we upgrade compilation kernels, cached entries don't silently change behavior.
03:18 Daniel: That seems like a lot of key entropy. Does it make keys too specific and hurt hit rates?
03:25 Marcus: It can. We offer layered keys: a primary strict key (full signature) and a fallback permissive key that drops non-critical bits (for instance drop runtime minor version) that can be used as a warm-start — but only for best-effort warming, not for authoritative correctness unless the customer opts-in.
03:47 Priya: About TTL: what's your default? We'll worry about staleness and incorrect behavior for conversation state.
03:54 Marcus: For system prompts we typically set long TTLs (1h–24h) depending on mutability. For session-specific prefixes tied to ephemeral metadata, TTLs are short (30s–2m) or we avoid caching them. We also support explicit invalidation APIs to evict keys if you rotate prompts.
04:15 Alice: How do you compute hit rate? We often see 'apparent' hit rate from cache lookup but not necessarily effective token savings.
04:23 Marcus: We report two metrics: lookup_hit_rate (cache lookups that returned an entry) and token_savings_hit_rate which accounts for how many input tokens were saved by cache reuse relative to baseline. The second is more meaningful for cost/throughput. E.g., a 70% lookup hit rate might yield only 30% token savings if hits are only for short prefixes.
04:43 Samir: We need to understand instrumentation for this. Will Redwood emit per-tenant hit counters and traces?
04:50 Marcus: Yes, for Dedicated and Private we emit per-tenant metrics: lookups, hits, token_savings, avg_latency_before_after. We can push these to your Prometheus/Grafana via metrics endpoint, and provide per-route dashboards in the Redwood Console.
05:06 Priya: On the topic of multi-tenant safety — what about cold-start noise and eviction policies causing carrier leaks? I mean, eviction could cause overlap in shared caches.
05:18 Marcus: That's why we recommend strict namespace tags for tenants by default. For shared pools you must mark entries as public and we maintain separate eviction pools. We also add per-entry ACL metadata in the cache store so we can audit which tenant created what. Note the ACL is metadata stored alongside the value and is enforced by the cache service. In Private deployments you can opt to store cache values on-disk encrypted with tenant-specific KMS keys.
05:40 Alice: Does encryption add latency?
05:43 Marcus: Minimal. We encrypt at rest and sign cache tokens. For per-request decryption, we use envelope encryption so the symmetric key is fetched once per container bootstrap and used locally — the KMS roundtrip is only for key wrapping/unwrapping at create time.
05:58 Daniel: How does caching interact with the runtime KV cache (the model KV cache for attention keys)? Could a prefix cache bypass the KV cache warmup?
06:08 Marcus: Good question. There are two layers: 1) the prefix/prompt cache that stores generated token sequences for a given prefix; 2) the model KV cache which stores past key/value tensors for autoregressive decoding. If the prefix cache returns a token sequence, we still need to hydrate the model's KV cache before serving decoder continuation to avoid cold attention; Redwood runtime either replays the cached token sequence through a fast KV-only pass to populate the KV cache (cheap) or stores serialized KV shard snapshots alongside the token sequence for instant attach. Storing KV snapshots increases storage size but reduces warmup latency.
06:44 Alice: Do you store KV snapshots for multi-GPU shards? We use long contexts and sharded KV.
06:50 Marcus: We can store per-shard serialized KV objects keyed by model_id+seq_len+prefix_key, but this is only supported in Dedicated/Private because it requires direct access to shard layout. For Hosted we do a replay by default.
07:06 Priya: What's the latency of the fast KV replay?
07:09 Marcus: In our test infra, replay for up to 2k tokens into the KV cache takes ~20–40ms on typical GPU setups vs 200–400ms full forward decode. With KV snapshot attach it's sub-10ms in ideal conditions.
07:27 Alice: Batch interactions: if we return a cached prefix for one request, can that request still be batched with live requests to improve throughput?
07:35 Marcus: Yes but batching semantics are more complex. Redwood's runtime supports mixed batches: requests that are cached-only or partially cached can be scheduled with live requests, but we must align sequence offsets. In practice we try to align to the point of continuation: all requests in a batch must share the same decoder step. That means sometimes cached warmups cause desynchronization and reduce batch efficiency. Our scheduler attempts to group compatible continuations to preserve throughput.
07:58 Daniel: Quantization — earlier you mentioned storing quantization tag in the key. Are there pitfalls with int8 vs int4 that change the validity of cached tokens?
08:07 Marcus: Yes. Lower-bit quantization can slightly change logits and sampling. So a cached token sequence produced by int8 may be incompatible with int4 policy. We recommend separate caches per quantization profile. In addition, for deterministic generation (greedy/beam) you still need to ensure tokenizer and sampling code match.
08:26 Priya: Any safety considerations around caching LLM outputs that might contain PII?
08:31 Marcus: Absolutely. We recommend PII filtering before caching. If the prompt can elicit PII, mark it non-cacheable. For Private deployments you can apply tenant-specific PII redaction rules or use on-write DLP hooks so entries containing sensitive patterns are never persisted.
08:48 Alice: How do you roll back a bad cache population? Suppose a buggy system prompt produced incorrect completions and they got cached across many keys.
08:56 Marcus: We have an invalidation API that supports prefix invalidation by hash pattern, and time-bounded rollback where you can delete all keys created between timestamps. We also keep a write-audit log that maps cache_key -> origin_request_id so you can trace and selectively evict.
09:09 Samir: For Private, where is the cache physically stored? Memory? Redis? Local SSD?
09:15 Marcus: Choice depends on performance needs. Options: in-memory distributed store for low latency (with replication for HA), SSD-backed LRU store for larger capacity (cold entries), or Redis-compatible stores for ease of ops. For Dedicated we often provision a Redis cluster with persistence; for the highest perf we use per-node in-memory shards with replication plus async persistence.
09:35 Priya: How do you do eviction when memory pressure is high? LRU? LFU? TTL-first?
09:40 Marcus: Default is hybrid: TTL-first eviction for known-expiring entries (session prefixes), then LRU within same TTL bucket, and a write-throttle to prevent cache stampede. We also have singleflight dedupe to ensure only one backend call populates a missed key.
09:56 Alice: Cache stampede — do you implement request coalescing?
10:00 Marcus: Yes singleflight and request coalescing at the cache layer. If many requests try to populate the same key, one will populate and the rest will wait or receive a partial warm-start. Also we use probabilistic early recomputation (small chance to refresh a hot key) to avoid thundering herd at TTL expiry.
10:20 Daniel: Observability — what traces do we need to validate correctness?
10:24 Marcus: You'll want per-request headers showing: cache_lookup_result (hit/miss), cache_key_hash, token_savings, kv_snapshot_attached (yes/no), attached_runtime_version. Redwood can optionally redact token payloads but emit hashes for verification.
10:39 Alice: Any special notes about VPC/on-prem?
10:43 Marcus: In Private deployments cache store can be colocated inside the customer's VPC. Network egress is minimal if cache is local. For hosted or Dedicated with VPC peering, ensure firewall allows cache ports and KMS access if you plan per-tenant envelope encryption. Some customers prefer sticky cache nodes per tenant to reduce cross-tenant blast radius.
11:00 Priya: What about GDPR/data residency?
11:03 Marcus: Cache data residency follows your deployment location. For multi-region routing we tag cache keys with region tag. We also support TTL policies per-region and per-tenant to purge data on request.
11:15 Alice: Benchmarks? You mentioned some numbers earlier.
11:19 Marcus: In our pre-call bench we ran 100k synthetic conversations with mix of short and long prefixes. Observed median token-savings latency improvement ~35% and tail (p95) latency improved by ~120ms when using KV snapshots. Lookup hit-rate varied widely by traffic: 55–82% for internal apps with high repetitiveness; token-savings rate was 28–60%. We'll share the spreadsheet.
11:41 Daniel: Let's talk SLOs — we need to keep worst-case latency under 350ms for the 95th percentile. Does caching break SLO accounting?
11:48 Marcus: No, caching improves SLOs in general but creates bimodal distribution: cache-hit path very fast, miss path unchanged. Your overall p95 should improve with sufficient hit rate, but ensure miss path still meets p95 target. We can implement graceful fallback to smaller models for overload to preserve p95 if you prefer.
12:05 Priya: Any gotchas around deployment upgrades? E.g., kernel selection changes, model compilation updates.
12:11 Marcus: Key thing is key partitioning — include compilation/kernel version in the strict key. Also provide migration tooling to invalidate old keys post-upgrade. We support rolling cache revalidation strategies to warm the new kernel without causing sudden miss spikes.
12:26 Alice: Ok good. Let's recap next steps.
12:29 Lara: Great recap — Marcus will share design doc and bench sheet, Alice will provide anonymized traces, Samir will check network bits, Lara will send pilot pricing. We'll target pilot start 2025-03-03.
12:45 Daniel: Thanks all.
12:47 Marcus: Thanks, will follow up with the doc and spreadsheet.
12:50 End of recording.
